topic: Setting up your office chair

slides.headline: Your office chair, set up in 5 minutes
slides.sub: Five quick adjustments. No new chair required.

slides.title: Start with seat height
slides.body: Feet flat on the floor, knees roughly level with or just below your hips. If your desk is too high for that, raise the chair and add a footrest or a sturdy box.

slides.title: Sit right back in the seat
slides.body: Scoot your hips to the back of the seat so the backrest can do some of the work. Leave a gap of two to three fingers between the seat edge and the back of your knees.

slides.title: Find your lower back support
slides.body: Set the lumbar support so it sits in the small of your back. No lumbar adjustment? A rolled-up hand towel behind your lower back works surprisingly well and costs nothing.

slides.title: Bring the armrests down
slides.body: Armrests set too high hitch your shoulders up towards your ears. Lower them, or take them off, so your elbows rest at about desk height with your shoulders relaxed.

slides.title: Then get out of it
slides.body: Even a well set-up chair gets uncomfortable after a couple of hours. Stand for calls, walk to refill your water and change position often. Variety matters more than any setting.

slides.headline: Still sore after the tweaks?
slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how you sit, move and work, then combine hands-on care with simple exercises you can do at your desk. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Five minutes with your office chair can make your workday feel a lot shorter.

Start with the seat height so your feet are flat and your knees sit about level with your hips. Sit right back so the backrest supports you, set the lumbar support into the small of your back (a rolled towel works too), and drop the armrests so your shoulders can relax.

Then remember the part most people skip: no chair is comfortable for eight hours straight. Standing for calls and short walking breaks usually do more than any adjustment lever.

If your back or neck is still grumbling, our chiropractors can assess how you sit and move and build a plan that includes exercise. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Returning to the gym after an injury

slides.headline: Your comeback plan for the gym
slides.sub: Start lighter, build steadily and let the next day guide you.

slides.title: Start at about half
slides.body: A common starting point is roughly half your usual weights and volume for the first week or two. It should feel easy. You're testing how the injured area responds, not proving anything.

slides.title: Use the 24-hour check
slides.body: Mild discomfort during a session is often fine. What matters more is the next morning. If pain or stiffness is clearly worse than usual after 24 hours, drop back a step.

slides.title: Change one thing at a time
slides.body: Add weight, sets or sessions, but not all three in the same week. Small, steady increases make it much easier to see what your body is ready for.

slides.title: Train around it, not through it
slides.body: Sore shoulder? Legs and trunk can still work hard. Cranky knee? Upper body sessions and swimming often feel fine. Staying active keeps your fitness and confidence ticking over.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Swelling that keeps coming back, a joint that gives way, pain that builds week to week, or numbness and tingling are worth an assessment before you push on.

slides.headline: Want a plan back to your lifts?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess the injury and how you train, then map out a return that fits your program. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Coming back to the gym after an injury? Ego is usually the first thing to leave at the door.

Most people do well starting at about half their usual weights and volume, then building up gradually. Mild discomfort during a set is often fine; the next-morning check tells you more. If things are clearly worse 24 hours later, drop back a step.

Change one variable at a time, and keep training the parts of you that aren't injured. Swelling that keeps returning, a joint that gives way or numbness and tingling are worth getting checked.

topic: Remedial massage for lower back pain: what to expect

slides.headline: Remedial massage for a sore lower back
slides.sub: What happens in the session and what to expect afterwards.

slides.title: It starts with questions
slides.body: Your remedial massage therapist will ask where it hurts, what eases or aggravates it, and about your health history. This helps them choose techniques and pressure that suit you.

slides.title: Where they'll usually work
slides.body: Lower back pain often involves the muscles around it too. Expect work through the back, glutes and hips, sometimes the upper thighs, with you comfortably draped throughout.

slides.title: Pressure is your call
slides.body: Firm doesn't have to mean painful. Your therapist should check in, and you can ask for lighter or firmer pressure at any time. Tense, braced muscles are harder to work on anyway.

slides.title: What it can and can't do
slides.body: Many people feel looser and move more easily for a day or two. Massage complements walking and strength work rather than replacing them, so keep moving between sessions.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg, numbness, weakness, changes to bladder or bowel control, or back pain after a fall should be assessed by a GP or physio before massage.

slides.headline: Ease the tension, keep moving
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists tailor each session to your back and work alongside our physios when rehab is needed. Book online — link in bio.

Your therapist starts by asking where it hurts, what eases it and what flares it. Then they'll usually work through the back, glutes and hips, because those muscles often join in when your lower back is sore. You stay draped the whole time, and pressure is always negotiable.

Realistic expectations help: many people feel looser for a day or two, and that's a great window to walk and do your exercises. Pain spreading down a leg, numbness or weakness should be checked first.

topic: Do you need a GP referral to see a physio?

slides.headline: Need a GP referral to see a physio?

slides.title: Private visits: no referral needed

slides.title: Medicare plan: yes, via your GP
slides.body: Medicare's GP chronic condition management plan can give a rebate for up to 5 allied health visits per calendar year. Your GP needs to set it up, and there's usually a gap fee.

slides.title: WorkCover and CTP claims

slides.body: If you have a DVA card, you'll usually need a referral from your GP or treating doctor before your first visit. Bring your card and the referral with you on the day.

slides.body: Send us a message or give us a call before you book. It's much easier to sort out paperwork beforehand than to find out something is missing on the day.

topic: Working from the couch: a better laptop setup

slides.headline: Working from the couch again?
slides.sub: You don't need a home office. A few swaps go a long way.

slides.title: The couch problem
slides.body: Soft cushions let you sink, and the laptop ends up on your knees. Your head drifts down towards the screen, and after an hour or so your neck and lower back let you know.

slides.title: Raise the screen
slides.body: Put the laptop on a firm cushion, a lap desk or a stack of books so the screen sits closer to eye level. Every few centimetres of height takes load off your neck.

slides.title: Add a cheap keyboard
slides.body: Once the screen is raised, typing gets awkward. A wireless keyboard and mouse let you keep the screen up and your arms relaxed. A small cost for a noticeable difference.

slides.title: Back into the corner
slides.body: Sit into the arm of the couch with a cushion behind your lower back, or move to the dining table for focused work. Changing spots through the day is a good thing.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading into an arm or leg, pins and needles, headaches that keep building, or stiffness that isn't easing after a week or two are worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Sore from the home office?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios look at your setup and how you move, then give you a simple plan to follow. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
The couch is comfy for the first 20 minutes. Then your neck starts talking. 🛋️

topic: Pilates and bone health

slides.headline: Bones love load. Where Pilates fits
slides.sub: How clinical Pilates can be part of a bone-friendly week.

slides.title: Bones respond to load
slides.body: Bone is living tissue that adapts to the forces placed on it. Current guidelines suggest regular resistance and weight-bearing exercise, progressed gradually, supports bone health.

slides.title: Where Pilates fits
slides.body: Reformer springs let you add resistance in small steps, which suits people new to strength work. Standing and single-leg exercises add weight-bearing and balance challenges.

slides.title: Balance matters too
slides.body: Better balance and leg strength can lower the chance of a fall. Clinical Pilates often includes standing work, step-ups and controlled single-leg exercises for exactly this reason.

slides.title: Pair it with other loading
slides.body: Pilates works well alongside walking, stair climbing and heavier strength training. Most people benefit from a mix across the week rather than relying on one type of exercise.

slides.title: Tell us about your bones
slides.body: If you've been told you have low bone density or osteoporosis, let us know. Some movements, like loaded deep forward bending, may be modified. Talk to your GP about medical management.

topic: Tight hips and glutes: massage plus movement

slides.headline: Massage for tight hips: half the answer
slides.sub: Massage can ease the tension. Movement helps it last.

slides.title: Tight is often tired
slides.body: Hips and glutes that feel tight are often under-used, or stuck working in one position all day. The feeling is real, even when your range of movement looks normal.

slides.title: What massage can do
slides.body: Remedial massage around the glutes, hips and lower back can ease tension and help you move more comfortably for a while. It's a helpful short-term tool, not the whole plan.

slides.title: Three moves after your session
slides.body: Try glute bridges, a figure-four stretch and side-lying leg lifts. Ten slow reps or a 30-second hold each, once or twice a day, helps keep things moving.

slides.title: Break up the sitting
slides.body: Stand and walk for a minute or two every half hour. Hips like variety, so switch between sitting, standing and moving through the day, even on busy desk days.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Groin pain, sharp catching or locking, pain that wakes you at night, or tingling down the leg is worth assessing with a physio or GP rather than massaging.

slides.headline: Ease it, then move it
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists work on the tension and send you home with simple moves to keep it easing. Book online — link in bio.

That tight feeling often comes from muscles that are tired or stuck in one position for hours. Remedial massage can ease the tension and help you move more freely for a while, and that's the perfect window to add some movement.

Try glute bridges, a figure-four stretch and side-lying leg lifts once or twice a day, and get up from your desk every half hour. Groin pain, catching or tingling down the leg are worth getting assessed first.

topic: Tailbone pain when sitting

slides.headline: Tailbone sore every time you sit?
slides.sub: Common, often slow to settle, and very manageable.

slides.title: What it usually is
slides.body: Tailbone pain, or coccydynia, often follows a fall onto the bottom, long stretches of sitting, or childbirth. Sometimes there's no clear trigger at all, and that's common too.

slides.title: Take the pressure off
slides.body: Try a wedge or U-shaped cushion with a cut-out at the back. Lean forward slightly when you sit so your weight goes through your sit bones instead of your tailbone.

slides.title: Stand up more often
slides.body: Pain often builds the longer you sit and spikes as you stand. Short, frequent breaks and a standing option for calls or reading can make the day much easier.

slides.title: Ease the muscles around it
slides.body: Tension in the pelvic floor and glutes can add to tailbone pain. Relaxed breathing, gentle stretches and soft glute work often help. A physio can guide what suits you.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a significant fall, pain that keeps getting worse, fevers, numbness, or changes to bladder or bowel control should be checked by your GP promptly.

slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess what's driving the pain and give you practical ways to sit, move and settle it. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Is it your hip or your back?

slides.headline: Is it your hip or your back?
slides.sub: They share muscles and nerves, so it's easy to mix them up.

slides.title: Why they're easy to confuse
slides.body: The hip and lower back sit close together and share muscles and nerve supply. Pain from one can be felt around the other, so where it hurts doesn't always tell you where it's from.

slides.title: Clues that lean towards the hip
slides.body: Pain in the groin or front of the hip, stiffness putting on socks, and discomfort turning the leg inwards often point towards the hip joint itself.

slides.title: Clues that lean towards the back
slides.body: Pain that changes with bending or long sitting, spreads into the buttock, or comes with lower back stiffness often involves the back. Plenty of people have a bit of both.

slides.title: How a chiro narrows it down
slides.body: Your chiropractor tests how the hip and back each move and respond to load. That guides a plan that may include hands-on care, adjustments and specific exercises.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness, leg weakness, changes to bladder or bowel control, fever, or pain after a fall should be seen by a GP promptly rather than waiting it out.

slides.headline: Stop guessing where it's from
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your hip and back together, and work alongside our physios when rehab is needed. Book online — link in bio.

Hip pain or back pain? Honestly, it can be hard to tell.

The hip and lower back share muscles and nerve supply, so pain from one is often felt in the other. Groin pain and trouble putting on socks tend to lean towards the hip. Pain that changes with bending or sitting and spreads into the buttock often involves the back. Many people have a bit of both.

A proper assessment tests each area so the plan targets the right thing. Numbness, weakness or bladder and bowel changes need prompt medical attention.

topic: Pilates and your pelvic floor

slides.headline: Your pelvic floor: more than squeezing
slides.sub: What clinical Pilates teaches about lifting, letting go and breathing.

slides.title: What the pelvic floor does
slides.body: It's a group of muscles at the base of your pelvis. They support the bladder and bowel, help with continence, and work together with your breathing and deep trunk muscles.

slides.title: Letting go matters too
slides.body: Pelvic floor muscles need to lift and relax. Some people hold too much tension, which can cause its own problems. Clinical Pilates teaches both the gentle lift and the release.

slides.title: Breathe with it
slides.body: As you breathe in, the pelvic floor gently lowers. As you breathe out, it lifts a little. Pilates uses this rhythm to time the effort of an exercise with your out-breath.

slides.title: Build it into real movement
slides.body: Once you can find the muscles, the aim is using them in daily tasks like squatting, lifting and getting out of the car. Reformer work lets you progress this gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Leaking, a heavy or dragging feeling, pelvic pain, or pain during intercourse are worth discussing with your GP or a pelvic health physiotherapist before starting a program.

slides.headline: Start with a Pilates assessment
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team checks how you move and breathe, then builds a program around you. Health fund cover varies, so check with your fund. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Pelvic floor training isn't just about squeezing as hard as you can.

These muscles support your bladder and bowel and work alongside your breath and deep trunk muscles. They need to lift, but they also need to let go, and some people hold far too much tension.

Clinical Pilates can help you coordinate the two: a gentle lift on the out-breath, a full release on the in-breath, then building that into squats, lifting and everyday movement. Leaking, heaviness or pelvic pain are worth discussing with your GP or a pelvic health physiotherapist first.

topic: Sacroiliac joint pain: what it is and what helps

slides.headline: Pain right by the dimple in your back?
slides.sub: Sacroiliac joint pain explained, minus the scary words.

slides.title: Meet the sacroiliac joint
slides.body: The SI joints link your spine to your pelvis, one on each side, near the dimples of your lower back. They're built for stability and only move a small amount.

slides.title: It isn't 'out of place'
slides.body: SI joints very rarely slip out. Pain there is usually about sensitivity and load, often after pregnancy, a fall, running, or a sudden jump in activity.

slides.title: What often aggravates it
slides.body: Standing on one leg, climbing stairs, rolling over in bed, getting out of the car, and long spells of standing or sitting are common triggers for SI joint pain.

slides.title: What tends to help
slides.body: Gradual strengthening for the glutes, hips and trunk usually leads the way. In the short term, pacing aggravating tasks and keeping your knees together getting out of the car can help.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain with fever, pain spreading down a leg with numbness or weakness, night pain that won't settle, or changes to bladder or bowel control need prompt medical review.

slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your back, hips and pelvis, then build a plan around strength and gradual loading. Book online — link in bio.

That sharp ache right next to the dimple in your lower back? It might involve your sacroiliac joint.

Gradual strength work for the glutes, hips and trunk usually helps most, with a bit of pacing while things settle. Fever, numbness, leg weakness or bladder and bowel changes need prompt medical review.

topic: Gardening without the sore back

slides.headline: Gardening without the Monday back
slides.sub: Enjoy the weekend garden and still move well come Monday.

slides.title: Warm up like it's sport
slides.body: Gardening is a genuine workout. A five-minute walk around the yard, a few squats and some gentle trunk turns get your body ready before the first bag of soil.

slides.title: Kneel, don't stoop
slides.body: Long periods bent over from the waist are a common cause of stiffness. Kneel on a pad, sit on a low stool, or use long-handled tools for weeding and planting.

slides.title: Switch jobs every 20 minutes
slides.body: Rotate between weeding, pruning, raking and carrying so no single position lasts too long. Stand up, lean back gently and walk for a minute between jobs.

slides.title: Lift close, turn with your feet
slides.body: Keep bags and pots close to your body, bend at your knees and hips, and turn with your feet rather than twisting. Use a wheelbarrow or split heavy loads in two.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg, numbness, weakness, or changes to bladder or bowel control need prompt medical attention. Stiffness that hasn't eased after a week or two is worth assessing.

slides.headline: Back in the garden, comfortably
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how you move, then combine hands-on care and exercise to help you stay active outdoors. Book online — link in bio.

Gardening is real physical work, so treat it that way. Warm up with a short walk and a few squats, kneel or use a low stool instead of stooping for long periods, and switch jobs every 20 minutes or so.

When lifting bags of soil or pots, keep them close, bend at the hips and knees and turn with your feet. A wheelbarrow is your friend. Some stiffness the next day is common, but pain down a leg, numbness or weakness need prompt attention.

topic: Forearm and wrist tension from mouse and keyboard

slides.headline: Your mouse hand deserves a break
slides.sub: Forearm and wrist tension from desk work, and what eases it.

slides.title: Small muscles, long hours
slides.body: Typing and mousing keep the forearm muscles gently working all day. They rarely get a proper break, so by Friday they can feel tight, achy or just plain tired.

slides.title: Check your desk setup
slides.body: Keep your elbows near your sides at about desk height and your wrists fairly flat. A mouse that fits your hand and a keyboard close to you cut down on reaching.

slides.title: Micro-breaks every half hour
slides.body: Drop your hands to your sides and shake them out, open and close your fists ten times, and gently stretch the wrists both ways. Thirty seconds is enough.

slides.title: Where remedial massage fits
slides.body: Massage through the forearms, upper arms and shoulders can ease tension and help your arms feel less heavy. It tends to work well combined with breaks and simple strength work.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness or tingling in the fingers, pain waking you at night, weakness or dropping things, or swelling are worth assessing with a physio or GP rather than massaging.

topic: Knee pain when kneeling: tradies and gardeners

slides.headline: Knees sore from kneeling all day?
slides.sub: For tradies, tilers, gardeners and anyone working low to the ground.

slides.title: Why kneeling bothers knees
slides.body: Kneeling puts pressure through the front of the knee, where a small fluid-filled sac called a bursa and the patellar tendon sit. Hours of it can leave them irritated.

slides.title: Pads are worth it
slides.body: Good-quality knee pads or a thick kneeling mat spread the pressure. Check the fit, because pads that slip leave the kneecap exposed. Replace them once the foam flattens.

slides.title: Change position often
slides.body: Alternate between kneeling on one knee, squatting, sitting on a low stool and standing. Aim to switch every 10 to 15 minutes so no single spot takes all the load.

slides.title: Strong thighs help
slides.body: Strengthening the quads and hips helps your knees handle getting up and down all day. Sit-to-stands, step-ups and wall sits a few times a week are a good starting point.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A hot, red or very swollen knee, fever, locking, giving way, or pain after a knock that doesn't settle is worth a prompt check with your GP or physio.

slides.headline: Keep your knees on the job
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your knees and work demands, then build a practical plan. Hurt at work? Bring your claim number.

caption:
Tradies, tilers and keen gardeners: how are your knees holding up?

Kneeling for hours puts steady pressure on the front of the knee, and it's a common source of soreness. Good knee pads that stay put, a thick mat, and switching between kneeling, squatting and a low stool every 10 to 15 minutes all help spread the load.

Stronger quads and hips make getting up and down easier too. A hot, red or very swollen knee, locking or giving way should be checked promptly.

topic: How private health extras rebates work

slides.headline: Extras cover, explained without the jargon
slides.sub: How health fund rebates for physio, chiro, Pilates and massage work.

slides.title: What extras cover is
slides.body: Extras, or ancillary, cover is the part of private health insurance that helps with services outside hospital, like physio, chiro and remedial massage. What's included depends on your policy.

slides.title: You pay, the fund rebates
slides.body: Your fund pays a set amount towards each eligible visit, and you pay the difference, known as the gap. Rebate amounts vary between funds and between policies.

slides.title: Annual limits apply
slides.body: Most policies cap how much you can claim for each service per year. Some limits are shared across several services, so physio and massage might draw from one pool.

slides.title: Claim on the spot with HICAPS
slides.body: If your extras cover includes the service, bring your health fund card and we can process the claim with HICAPS at the end of your visit. You just pay the gap.

slides.title: Questions to ask your fund
slides.body: Which services are covered? What's the rebate per visit? What's my annual limit, and is it shared? Are there waiting periods? Is clinical Pilates covered on my policy?

slides.headline: Know your cover, then book
slides.body: Bring your health fund card and we'll claim with HICAPS on the day. Book online — link in bio.

topic: High hamstring pain when sitting

slides.headline: Sit bone pain: why stretching can backfire
slides.sub: High hamstring tendon pain is common in runners and desk workers.

slides.title: What's often going on
slides.body: The hamstring tendons attach to your sit bone. When they're overloaded, they can become sensitive and sore, especially with long sitting, hill running, lunges or deep stretching.

slides.title: Go easy on the stretching
slides.body: Hamstring stretches press the tendon against the bone and often aggravate this pain. It's usually worth pausing deep hamstring stretches for a few weeks while things settle.

slides.title: Sit smarter for now
slides.body: Choose firmer chairs, try a folded towel under your thighs so less pressure goes through the sit bones, and get up regularly. Long drives and low couches are common aggravators.

slides.title: Load it gradually
slides.body: Tendons respond to steady, progressive strength work. Physios often start with holds such as bridges or hamstring isometrics, then build to heavier and faster exercises over weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sudden pop or bruising at the back of the thigh, numbness or tingling down the leg, or pain that keeps getting worse is worth an assessment soon.

slides.headline: Get your hamstring back on track
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess the tendon and build a loading plan that fits your running or work week. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Your first remedial massage: what happens

slides.headline: Booked your first remedial massage?

slides.title: Before: a quick health check
slides.body: Expect a short form and some questions about your health, injuries and what you'd like help with. Mention pregnancy, recent surgery, medications or any skin conditions.

slides.title: You're in control of draping
slides.body: You only undress to your comfort level. Your therapist leaves the room while you get on the table, and you stay covered with towels except for the area being worked on.

slides.title: Pressure you can adjust
slides.body: Remedial massage can be firm, but it shouldn't make you hold your breath. Your therapist will check in, and you can ask for lighter or firmer pressure at any time.

slides.title: Afterwards: what's normal
slides.body: You might feel loose, a little tired, or mildly sore for a day or two. Drink some water, keep moving gently, and tell your therapist how you pulled up next time.

slides.body: If your extras cover includes remedial massage, you can claim on the spot with HICAPS and pay only the gap. It's worth checking your policy's limits beforehand.

topic: Moving house: lift smarter, not harder

slides.headline: Moving house? Lift smarter, not harder
slides.sub: A back-friendly plan for moving day and the week before it.

slides.title: Pack smaller boxes
slides.body: Heavy items like books go in small boxes, and light things like linen go in big ones. Aim for boxes you can lift comfortably without holding your breath.

slides.title: Warm up before the first load
slides.body: A few minutes of walking, squats and gentle trunk turns prepares your body for a big day. Moving house is a full-body workout, so treat it like one.

slides.title: Keep it close
slides.body: Hold boxes close to your body, bend at the hips and knees, and pivot with your feet rather than twisting. Use a trolley for anything awkward or heavy.

slides.title: Pace the day
slides.body: Take short breaks every hour, drink water and eat properly. Strains often happen when people are tired and rushing the last few loads. Share heavy lifts with a mate.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain spreading down a leg, numbness, weakness, or changes to bladder or bowel control need prompt medical attention. Stiffness that hasn't eased after a week is worth assessing.

slides.headline: Sore after the big move?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess how you move, then combine hands-on care and exercise to help you settle into the new place. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Forefoot pain and burning toes (Morton's neuroma)

slides.headline: Burning between your toes when you walk?
slides.sub: Forefoot pain and Morton's neuroma, in plain English.

slides.title: What it usually is
slides.body: Morton's neuroma is an irritated, thickened nerve between the long bones of the foot, most often between the third and fourth toes. It's common and often settles with simple changes.

slides.title: What it often feels like
slides.body: Burning, tingling or numbness into the toes, or a feeling like standing on a pebble or a folded sock. Taking your shoe off and rubbing the foot often eases it.

slides.title: Give your toes room
slides.body: Narrow, pointed or high-heeled shoes squeeze the forefoot. Try shoes with a wider toe box, a lower heel and decent cushioning, and loosen the laces across the front.

slides.title: Other things that can help
slides.body: A metatarsal pad placed just behind the sore spot can spread the pressure. Adjusting your walking or running load, plus calf and foot strength work, often helps too.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Constant numbness, swelling or redness, pain that wakes you at night, or symptoms that aren't easing after a few weeks of shoe changes are worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Walk more comfortably again
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your feet, footwear and loading, then build a plan to settle your symptoms. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Feels like you're walking on a pebble, or a folded sock, under the ball of your foot?

Start with your shoes: a wider toe box, a lower heel and laces loosened across the front give the forefoot room. A metatarsal pad, adjusting your walking or running load, and calf and foot strengthening can help too. Constant numbness, swelling or night pain are worth getting checked.
